title: Surfer's Guide for the Perplexed (Jonah on the Raging Sea)
program_note:
To catch a wave, a surfer must be at the right place, at the right time, and must have the willingness to commit.  If the surfer is too early, too late, or does not commit to being in the path of the wave, then the wave will either pass right by or come crashing down.  Once out in the surf, though, attempting to avoid the waves can only be successful some of the time:  eventually the waves will overtake the surfer.

The same may be said of righteousness or charity.  To do a charitable act, the righteous person must be at the right place at the right time, and must have the willingness to commit to righteousness.  If the act of charity is too early, too late, or is not backed by the fullest commitment, then such charity may have no positive effect, or may actually have a negative effect.  Attempting to avoid the responsibility of righteousness can only be successful some of the time:  eventually the force of opportunity knocking will overtake the uncommitted person.

This allegorical response to the story of Jonah is portrayed musically by the inevitability and inexorability of the waves, which ultimately come crashing down about half-way through the composition.  After some time in the depths of despair, Jonah, the  surfer on the waves of righteousness, learns the power and importance of commitment, finally taking that beautiful long ride on the waves.
